bp: A web crawler is a machine that starts from known web addresses, follows links, and brings back pages so a search, monitoring, or news service can know what exists. In an editorial crawl, the aim is not merely to download many pages. The crawler needs broad coverage, meaning it should find many distinct publications, and freshness, meaning it should find new material early enough to matter. It also has strict limits. Politeness rules prevent hammering sites, and request budgets cap how many starts or page fetches can be spent. URLBank serves the upstream decision before ordinary search ranking happens: which entry points are worth giving crawl budget to today. The paper argues that production crawlers often still depend on manual seed management, where people maintain lists of starting points. That manual habit wastes work on redundant seeds and misses high-yield ones. URLBank replaces that habit with a controller learned from the crawler's own temporal telemetry.
wh: The hard part is that a seed's value is not visible from its address alone. Two starting points may look different but lead to the same set of pages, so choosing both spends scarce requests twice for little extra coverage. Another seed may look quiet most of the time but repeatedly reveals new publications early. A crawler also revisits sites in cycles, called revolutions in the abstract, so the system must care about time: which links persist, which disappear, and which entry points keep producing first-seen pages across repeated crawls. A simple count of pages reached can be misleading because it may reward seeds that mostly rediscover already known pages. A simple freshness rule can be misleading if the links are unstable and cannot be counted on later. URLBank must therefore balance coverage, freshness, stability, and efficiency while respecting the same request budget and politeness conditions as the production crawler.
naive: A smart beginner would ask human editors or crawl operators to list important site sections, then give each section a roughly fixed amount of crawl attention. If results look poor, they might add more seeds or keep the ones that historically returned many pages. This fails in two concrete ways described by the abstract. First, it oversamples redundant seeds: several starting points can lead to the same content, so the crawler feels busy while adding little new coverage. Second, it misses high-yield seeds that are not obvious to humans but repeatedly expose new publications. The beginner's rule treats seed value as a static property, when the useful evidence is in repeated crawl behavior over time.
ap: URLBank's central move is to treat seed selection as a measured allocation problem rather than a hand-maintained list. It reads temporal crawl telemetry: records from past crawler revolutions showing which links appeared, persisted, and led to first-seen publications. From those records it identifies candidate entry points and gives them two interpretable measurements. Stability asks whether links remain present across revolutions, so the crawler is not betting heavily on vanishing paths. Productivity asks how often a candidate leads to publications that had not been seen before. Then URLBank ranks candidates by greedy marginal gain on a shared-credit coverage objective. In plain terms, each seed gets credit for the new coverage it adds beyond what already chosen seeds cover, and overlapping seeds must share credit rather than each claiming the same pages. The system builds a ranked prefix of seeds for a given budget.
mech: The mechanism begins with crawl telemetry collected from repeated visits to many sites. Each record says something about links observed during crawler revolutions and about whether following a route produced first-seen publications. URLBank first turns that history into candidate entry points, which are possible seeds the crawler could start from or prioritize. For each candidate, it estimates stability by checking persistence: does the link or route remain available across repeated crawls, or does it appear only briefly? It estimates productivity by measuring the rate at which the candidate leads to new publications, not merely pages already known. Next, the system considers coverage as a shared resource. If two candidates lead to the same publications or overlapping regions of a site, both should not receive full independent credit. The shared-credit objective assigns value to unique or useful coverage while reducing duplicate reward. The ranking then proceeds greedily: choose the candidate that adds the largest extra gain to the current chosen set, update what is already covered, and repeat until the Top-K or budget limit is reached. The output is not just one best seed. It is an ordered list of prefixes, so production can allocate larger or smaller crawl budgets transparently.
math: The main mathematical object is a temporal link graph. The nodes are web locations or pages, the links are observed connections between them, and time matters because the same link can persist, disappear, or newly appear across crawler revolutions. Graph reasoning fits because a seed's value comes from where its outgoing paths lead, not just from the seed's own address. The second idea is estimation from repeated observations. Stability and productivity are not magic labels; they are summaries of history. Stability estimates how often a link remains available over repeated cycles. Productivity estimates how often following a candidate produces first-seen publications. The third idea is ranking under a budget: many candidates exist, but only the top few can receive requests. URLBank converts several measurements into an order. The fourth idea is greedy marginal gain. Greedy means the system repeatedly picks the next candidate with the best immediate extra value. Marginal gain means the value is measured after accounting for what previous picks already covered. Shared credit is the key guardrail: when several seeds reach the same content, their duplicated reach is counted less than unique reach. The tradeoff is speed and interpretability versus perfect global search; the greedy rule is simple, auditable, and practical at web scale.
dots: This paper connects web crawling to the broader retrieval and ranking family. Search papers usually ask which documents to show after a query; URLBank asks an earlier question, which web entry points should be collected before downstream retrieval is possible. It also connects to efficiency and scalability work because the scarce resource is explicit: polite requests and crawl budget. The system must get more coverage and freshness without spending more requests. Its temporal link graph links it to network reasoning papers, where relationships carry evidence and repeated structure matters. Its use of stability and productivity links it to sequence and temporal information access: the system trusts patterns seen across crawler revolutions, not a frozen snapshot. Finally, its greedy shared-credit objective connects to allocation problems across the conference, where the central move is choosing a small useful subset from a large pile while avoiding duplicate spending. URLBank is therefore a ranking method for upstream attention, not a page relevance method.
ww: URLBank should improve over manual seed management because it uses the crawler's own history to expose patterns humans cannot reliably maintain by hand. If a seed repeatedly discovers new publications early, productivity gives it upward pressure. If a seed's links persist across revolutions, stability says the crawler can rely on it. If a seed reaches mostly the same material as another stronger seed, shared credit reduces its apparent value. That last point matters: a crawler budget is wasted not only by bad seeds, but by good-looking seeds that duplicate each other. The greedy marginal-gain loop directly attacks that waste because each new selection is judged against the set already chosen. The method also works operationally because its scores are interpretable. Operators can see which prefixes are ranked for a budget, diagnose health, version policies, and reverse changes if needed. The shadow A/B result over 5,238 sites supports the intuition: under identical conditions, better seed ordering produced higher coverage, greater efficiency, and earlier discovery.
po: The payoff is a more disciplined way to spend crawl attention. Under the same production conditions, URLBank reports higher coverage, greater efficiency, and earlier discovery than manual seed curation in a shadow A/B evaluation across 5,238 sites. The abstract also says gains stay stable across Top-K budgets and approach near-complete coverage with far fewer seeds. In deployment with Meltwater's Pulitzer crawler, the ranked prefixes, versioned policies, and health diagnostics make the allocation visible and reversible. That matters in industrial crawling because operators need improvement without turning crawl policy into an opaque black box.
limits: The method assumes past crawl telemetry is a useful guide to future crawl value. If a site changes its structure sharply, blocks the crawler, or starts publishing in a new section with no history, stability and productivity may lag behind reality. Shared credit also depends on correctly observing overlap; if telemetry misses paths, duplicate or unique coverage can be misestimated. The abstract reports a large shadow A/B study and production deployment details, but it does not prove behavior on every type of website, adversarial site, language, or news cycle. Greedy marginal gain is practical and interpretable, yet it can miss combinations whose joint value is better than any seed's immediate extra value.
